title: Go forth (Genesis 12:1–3)
hook: Abram is told to leave land, birthplace and father's house for a place not yet named

segments.voice: Yesterday: Babel, a city built to make a name, and a scattering into many languages.

Abram is seventy-five, settled in a city called Haran, with a household and possessions gathered around him. His father's house is there. Everything he knows is there. Then God speaks, and in the old JPS translation it sounds like this: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto the land that I will show thee." That's it. No map, no address, not even the name of the place. Just: go, and I'll show you when you get there. People still set out like this, on a job offer or a hunch, without knowing the street they'll end up on.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, AND SETTLED.` → `GET THEE OUT.` → `A LAND NOT YET NAMED.`

segments.voice: Lech lecha. Lech means go. Lecha means, literally, to you, or for you. So the plainest translation is just go, but the Hebrew has that strange little extra: go for yourself. Rashi, the medieval commentator, reads it as go for your own good: this journey is for you. Later Hasidic teachers read it more boldly: go to yourself. The outward journey is also an inward one. Now look at the order: your country, your birthplace, your father's house. If you were actually leaving, you'd walk out of your father's door first, then the town, then the country. The Torah lists it from the widest to the closest, and commentators notice that each step cuts nearer to the heart. The hardest thing to leave comes last. Then the promise: I will make of thee a great nation, and bless thee, and make thy name great; and, the verse ends, "in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed." Remember Babel? The builders said, let us make us a name. Here God says, I will make thy name great. What they tried to grab is given as a gift, to someone who walks away from everything to receive it. And Abram goes. The Torah doesn't tell us how he felt. The Mishnah says Abraham was tested ten times, and later rabbis count this call among the tests. The same two words, lech lecha, come back later in his story, at the binding of Isaac. For now, he simply goes before he knows.
screen: `GO — FOR YOURSELF.` · `WIDEST TO CLOSEST.` · `BABEL GRABBED A NAME; THIS IS A GIFT.` · `ONE OF TEN TESTS.` · then, large: `ALL THE FAMILIES OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Think of one path you walk every day without deciding to: the same street to work, the same aisle in the store, the same chair, the first app you open. Picture taking a different way, just once, and stay with the small unease of not knowing what's around the corner. If you pray, you can ask for courage for one small step.
Lech lecha. Go, for yourself, or go to yourself. The call that starts Abram's journey, and the name of this Torah portion.
Your line: go before you know. Abram had a call, not a map. That's day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Lech Lecha is the name of the weekly Torah portion that begins with this call, read in synagogues each autumn, and its opening words are often quoted for anyone setting out on a move or a new stage of life.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens "Imagine" and no longer gives Abram "land and flocks" (the text says possessions and souls gotten in Haran); dropped the leaving-for-college line that echoed day 29's hook; "last and hardest test" and "only once more" softened (Avot 5:3 counts ten tests but does not list them).
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 12:1 and 12:3.
12:2 is paraphrased close to the JPS wording ('I will make of thee a great nation, and bless thee, and make thy name great'); it is not marked as a quotation. Confirm acceptable.
'Go to yourself' is a common Hasidic reading (often attributed to the Zohar or later Hasidic masters); left unattributed. Confirm.
Order country / birthplace / father's house read as widest to closest: a common commentary theme (e.g. Ramban/Akedat Yitzchak). Confirm.
Ten tests of Abraham: Pirkei Avot 5:3; lists vary on which is first (some begin with the furnace of Ur). The script says 'among the ten tests' for that reason.
Lech lecha only in 12:1 and 22:2: confirm.
